chunks: From him, from several of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayd, from Abu Sahl al-Qurashi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the meat of the dog, and he said, 'It is masakh (transformed/dispensed with).' I said, 'Is it haram (forbidden)?' He said, 'It is najas (impure).' I repeated the question three times, and each time he said, 'It is najas (impure).'

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdillah; title of Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.مَسْخٌ: Masakh; transformed or dispensed with, often used for meat that is not like normal animal flesh

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on dog meat in Shia fiqh: is it haram or najas?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the ontological status of dog meat as *masakh* (transformed or distinct from standard livestock) and its legal status as *najas* (ritually impure). The repetition of 'najas' three times underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on its physical impurity, which necessitates purification of any vessel it touches, rather than merely its prohibition due to lack of proper slaughter (*dhikr*). This clarification helps jurists differentiate between *haram* (forbidden to eat) and *najas* (impure), a key distinction in Shia fiqh regarding food purity.
